title: MAC, HMAC and AEAD
syllabusUnit: Unit IV: Message Authentication Codes & HMAC
learningGoals: You will be able to explain why a hash alone does NOT provide message authentication.
You will be able to diagram the HMAC nested hashing structure with ipad and opad.
You will be able to distinguish CMAC from HMAC.

lessonCards.title: Why Hashes Need Keys: The MAC
lessonCards.analogy: A seal on a letter: anyone can press wax, but only a king with the royal signet ring can stamp a valid seal.
lessonCards.coreConcept: A hash function has no secret key: an attacker can alter the message and recompute a valid hash! A Message Authentication Code (MAC) mixes in a secret key.
lessonCards.example: MAC = H(Key || Message) ensures only parties holding the secret key can generate or verify the tag.

lessonCards.title: The HMAC Construction (RFC 2104)
lessonCards.analogy: Double-wrapping a package with two layers of tape and two distinct secret key stamps.
lessonCards.coreConcept: HMAC(K, M) = H((K XOR opad) || H((K XOR ipad) || M)). This nested structure completely defeats length-extension attacks that break simple H(K || M).
lessonCards.example: ipad = 0x36 repeating; opad = 0x5C repeating. Used in AWS API signatures and JWT authentication tokens.

lessonCards.title: CMAC & Authenticated Encryption
lessonCards.analogy: A lock that encrypts and seals in one swift turn, instead of locking then taping separately.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Cipher-based MAC (CMAC) builds a secure MAC using a block cipher like AES. Authenticated Encryption (AES-GCM) integrates encryption and MAC into a single unified pass.
lessonCards.example: Avoids the 'Encrypt-and-MAC' vs 'MAC-then-Encrypt' vulnerabilities that plagued older SSL versions.

questions.prompt: Why is sending a standard hash H(M) alongside message M insufficient to guarantee message authenticity?
options: An attacker in the middle can alter M to M' and simply recalculate H(M') to match
Hashes can only be sent on Saturdays
questions.explanation: Because standard hash functions like SHA-256 use NO secret keys; anyone can calculate a valid hash for any altered payload.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Without a secret key, an attacker recomputes the hash after tampering.
256 bits is plenty long, but lacks a secret key.
Time of transmission is irrelevant.
Hashes produce pseudo-random non-zero digests.
questions.realWorldExample: This is why message integrity requires a shared secret key (HMAC) or a private key (Digital Signature).

questions.prompt: In the HMAC formula HMAC(K, M) = H((K XOR opad) || H((K XOR ipad) || M)), what are 'ipad' and 'opad'?
options: Fixed constant padding byte sequences (0x36 and 0x5C) that create two distinct derived keys
Random numbers that change on every message
questions.explanation: ipad (inner pad, byte 0x36 repeated) and opad (outer pad, byte 0x5C repeated) ensure the inner and outer hash passes use cryptographically independent subkeys.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Constant byte masks that decorrelate inner and outer hashing rounds.
They are defined RFC 2104 constants, not user passwords.
They have zero relation to consumer hardware.
They are fixed constants, not dynamic nonces.
questions.realWorldExample: Mihir Bellare, Ran Canetti, and Hugo Krawczyk designed HMAC in 1996; it remains uncompromised today.

questions.prompt: What vulnerability affects naive hash constructions like H(Key || Message) in Merkle-Damgård hashes?
questions.explanation: In Merkle-Damgård hashes, an attacker can append data to the message and extend the hash state without knowing the secret key.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Length-extension allows attackers to forge valid authentication tags for extended payloads.
Avalanche properties are preserved.
Bit flips are detected.
Buffer overflow is a memory safety flaw, not an algorithmic hash flaw.
questions.realWorldExample: Flickr API suffered a vulnerability where API signatures using H(Secret || Params) were forged via length-extension.

questions.prompt: What does a Cipher-based Message Authentication Code (CMAC) use as its underlying building block?
options: A symmetric block cipher like AES
questions.explanation: NIST SP 800-38B defines CMAC, which builds a secure MAC using a block cipher (AES) in a CBC-like construction with subkey derivation.
wrongExplanations: Correct! CMAC uses AES to generate authentication tags.
RSA is used for asymmetric digital signatures.
RNGs generate randomness, not authentication tags.
Text files store data.
questions.realWorldExample: CMAC is widely used in automotive CAN bus networks and IPsec.

questions.prompt: When combining encryption and authentication, which order is proven to be the most secure according to modern cryptography?
questions.explanation: Encrypt-then-MAC encrypts plaintext first, then computes a MAC over the ciphertext. The receiver verifies the MAC before touching decryption, preventing oracle attacks.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Encrypt-then-MAC prevents padding oracles because invalid packets are dropped before decryption.
MAC-then-Encrypt was used in legacy TLS and caused POODLE and Lucky13 attacks.
Encrypt-and-MAC was used in SSH and can leak plaintext equality.
Authenticated encryption is strictly required.
questions.realWorldExample: Modern AEAD ciphers like AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 inherently implement Encrypt-then-MAC internally.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the 'Associated Data' in Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD)?
options: Data like packet headers that must be authenticated for integrity, but left unencrypted so routers can inspect it
questions.explanation: Network routers need to read IP headers to forward packets, so headers are authenticated to prevent tampering, but left unencrypted.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Associated Data is verified for integrity without being encrypted.
Images are payload data.
Passwords are never sent in Associated Data.
Cache files are OS storage.
questions.realWorldExample: In TLS 1.3, sequence numbers and record headers are authenticated as Associated Data in AES-GCM.

ashRecap: A hash proves data wasn't accidentally corrupted, but a MAC proves it wasn't maliciously forged by an attacker holding no key!
